name: Aristocracy
scope: Aristocracy as a form of government and the political ideal behind it: rule by a small class of those held best qualified, governing in the interest of the whole (Britannica, s2; Aristotle's account in the IEP and SEP entries, s4 and s5). Aristotle's version, rule of the morally and intellectually superior few for the common good, is the classical core (s2, s3, s8, s9); Plato's perfect state of philosopher-rulers selected by education is its best-known statement (s3, s6, s10). Encyclopedia.com (s3) adds modern forms: hereditary aristocracies that alternated with absolute monarchy until the French Revolution, the claim of Burke, Nietzsche and others that every people is governed by an elite and that all civilization is the work of aristocracies, and proposals for an aristocracy of talent. Ludovici's 1915 'A Defence of Aristocracy' (s7) is kept as a primary modern statement of the principle that the best should rule, by a hereditary class. Britannica (s2) and Encyclopedia.com (s3) also use the word for the social class of nobles; this audit takes that class only as far as the sources tie its rule to the doctrine. The corrupt form, oligarchy or rule of the few in their own interest, is treated by the sources as aristocracy's opposite. Excluded: the downloaded books that only list or describe noble families and their manners (Walford's County Families, Vadivelu's Aristocracy of Southern India, Stewart's Glasgow citizenship, Vehse's Austrian court memoirs, Loewy's Manners of the Aristocracy) and Wade's Extraordinary Black Book, an attack on the British establishment, since none is a defining source or a text of the doctrine; Marxist 'labor aristocracy' (a separate catalog entry); and the broader entries on elitism, oligarchy and monarchism.

democracy-best.rationale: Aristotle ranks democracy among the flawed regimes, below aristocracy, and in Plato's Republic Book VIII democracy is the regime that gives way to tyranny; the rule of the best few is the doctrine's core.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Aristotle (Politics IV) calls appointment by lot a democratic device and election the mark of the aristocratic or constitutional state, which draws from each element the principle of election.

experts-over-public.rationale: Plato's Republic, as read in Ferrari's introduction to the Griffith edition (on Book VI, 488a-e), makes rule a matter of knowledge like a helmsman's rather than of persuading the populace; Ludovici asks why 'the men who know' have no say. Both put policy with the qualified few.

natural-rulers.rationale: Ludovici (Chapter I and the chapter on heredity) holds that fitness to rule is a matter of the body inherited from one's ancestors, not of chance or upbringing; Plato says philosophers must become kings.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Ludovici's Defence of Aristocracy (Chapter VIII and the introductory argument) contends that the hereditary principle is an essential condition of an aristocracy and a good principle; Britannica notes aristocracies have mostly been hereditary.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Plato's Republic (Book 2, 377b ff.) has the founders supervise the storytellers and reject most of the stories nurses and mothers tell, to shape the guardians' character.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Aristotle (Politics IV) describes the aristocratic or constitutional state as taking one element from each of oligarchy and democracy, while Plato's best state is rule by the philosopher-rulers alone, so the sources split.

summary: Aristocracy holds that political power belongs to a small class of those best qualified to rule, who govern for the good of the whole rather than their own advantage. In Plato and Aristotle the best are chosen by virtue, wisdom and training, and democracy ranks below the rule of the few; later defenders such as Ludovici argue that the fit to rule are bred, so that a hereditary governing class is a good principle. Its corrupt form is oligarchy, rule of the few for themselves.
